passage:
Naveen, I swear, Farhan sir hates me. Every time I send him something he replies in one line: 'Fine.' 'Fix slide 4.' 'Noted.' No hello, no thanks. With the other interns he jokes, but with me it's all business. So I just keep my head down in meetings and don't say anything. Why give him more to dislike?
Then yesterday Rimjhim told me he'd asked her, 'Is Sanjana even interested in this role? She never asks a single question.' Interested? I'm staying back till eight!
I thought quiet meant respectful. He thinks it means I don't care. And I thought short meant he hates me. Maybe it just means he's drowning in emails, like everyone. I don't know.

qa.q: How late does Sanjana say she is staying back?
qa.a: She is staying back till eight.

qa.q: Why has Sanjana been keeping her head down in meetings?
qa.a: She believes Farhan sir dislikes her because of his one-line replies, so she stays quiet to avoid giving him more reasons.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Sanjana now that she knows how her silence looks?
qa.a: She could ask a question or two in the next meeting, or tell Farhan sir she is keen to learn, so he stops reading her silence as lack of interest.

qa.q: How does Farhan sir seem to see Sanjana's silence?
qa.a: He seems to read it as lack of interest, not realising she is quiet out of respect and fear, and he may not notice how brisk his replies sound.

grounding: A woman intern reads her male senior's brisk replies as dislike while he reads her silence as disinterest.

passage: I'm Lakshmi, and I sit between Bidisha's desk and Mr Rao's cabin at the accounts firm, so I see both sides. Mr Rao talks to everyone in bullet points: 'Ledger. Today. Thanks.' He doesn't mean anything by it; he's been like that for fifteen years. But Bidisha, who joined in June, flinches every time. She's stopped asking him anything and just quietly guesses. Last week in the tea room Mr Rao said to me, 'That new girl doesn't seem very interested. Never asks a thing.' The same afternoon Bidisha whispered, 'He can't stand me, can he?' I didn't know what to tell either of them. I think they're both wrong. Nobody explains, and nobody asks.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's whisper 'He can't stand me, can he?' reveal about how she reads Mr Rao?
qa.a: She takes his brisk bullet-point style as personal dislike, and she seems anxious and hurt by it.

qa.q: How could someone like Lakshmi gently help at this stage?
qa.a: She could tell Bidisha that Mr Rao talks this way to everyone and encourage her to ask, or mention to him that the new joiner may need more explanation.

qa.q: How does Mr Rao see Bidisha's quietness?
qa.a: He reads her silence as lack of interest, not realising his short style has made her afraid to ask.

grounding: A colleague sees a senior read a new woman's silence as disinterest while she reads his brisk tone as dislike.
